msg: The last section of Paper 49 describes the various ways mortals leave the inhabited worlds and go on to the mansion worlds. There are those who sleep as a group and awaken at the dispensational roll calls, those who awaken individually on the third day, and the order addressed in today's passage, the mortals of the probationary-dependent orders of ascension. This last order is made up of children and youths who die young, before choosing the Paradise career for themselves.

The passage first declares a very important principle: the arrival of an Adjuster constitutes identity in the eyes of the universe. The moment the spirit of God comes to indwell a child, that child is registered in the records of the universe as a personal identity and is placed on the roll calls of justice. Even if the child is still too young to have made any great decision, he or she is never forgotten or abandoned. The universe does not measure the worth of a personality by age or achievement.

Temporal life on the evolutionary worlds is uncertain. Through accident, illness, and the unforeseen, many leave this world early. No words in the world can fully console parents who have lost a child. But The Urantia Book tells us that such children follow the parent of most advanced spiritual status, going on to the system finaliter world, the probationary nursery. The passage that follows explains that even younger children, who die before receiving an Adjuster, are repersonalized on the mansion worlds when one of their parents arrives there (see 49:6.12).

This teaching shows how tender is the love of the Universal Father. God has prepared a way even for young souls who never had the chance to choose for themselves. They are nurtured and grow up in the nursery, and in due time they receive the opportunity to choose the eternal path for themselves. Here we also find that the spiritual progress of the parents is linked to the destiny of their children. When parents grow in faith, it is not for themselves alone but also for the children they love.

This truth gives new meaning to the raising of children. Parents are not merely people who feed bodies and teach knowledge; they are partners who help a personality indwelt by the spirit of God to meet truth and love for the first time. Every moment in which a child learns honesty, learns to care for others, and comes to know how to call God Father is a time in which that young soul is growing. The Urantia Book stresses again and again that the family is the most important institution of human society (see Paper 84). When we treat a child as an eternal being, our tone of voice, our patience, and our waiting are changed. And a child who has grown up so loved, whether he lives long on this earth or stays only a short while, will go on growing without interruption in the embrace of the Universal Father.

Today, look upon the young lives around you with new eyes. The spirit of God already dwells in those small bodies; they are eternal personalities whose names the universe knows. And if there is someone you have already lost, place them in God's hands and devote yourself to growing spiritually first. That is the best way to prepare for the day you will meet again. In the love of the Universal Father no life vanishes in vain, and even a short life becomes a precious first chapter of an eternal story.
d099.pr: Treat one child near you with special care today, as an eternal personality whose name God knows.

msg: Paper 50 sets out in seven ages the stages through which the civilization of a normal world develops under the rule of a Planetary Prince. After the age of food, the age of security, the age of material comfort, the age of the quest for knowledge and wisdom, and the age of philosophy and brotherhood, it arrives at the sixth, the age of spiritual striving, of which today's passage speaks. And beyond it awaits the age of light and life.

This sequence mirrors not only the development of civilization but also the growth of a single person. We too first struggle to solve the problems of making a living and staying safe, then look for comfort and enjoyment, and go on to learning and reflection. Then at some moment we feel a deep thirst that material, intellectual, and social satisfactions alone cannot quench. The passage calls this attaining those levels of personal insight which impel us to seek for spiritual satisfactions and cosmic understandings. If that thirst has come to you, it is a sign that your soul is being called to the next stage.

In this age religion undergoes a great change. It is completing the ascent from the emotional domains of fear and superstition to the high levels of cosmic wisdom and personal spiritual experience. It moves from primitive religion, which sought to appease the gods to escape punishment, to a religion of experience that knows the loving Father directly and enjoys fellowship with him. Education aspires not to mere information but to the attainment of meanings, and culture grasps at cosmic relationships and true values.

The last sentence of the passage describes the people of this age as genuinely cultured, truly educated, and exquisitely God-knowing. True culture and education are not separate from knowing God. An intellect that knows much but does not know God is not yet complete, while one who knows God deeply, however little schooling he may have, has already grasped what matters most. The religion Jesus showed us was just such a living religion of experience (see Paper 101).

There is one more important lesson hidden in the order of these seven ages: we cannot ignore the earlier stages and leap all at once into the spiritual age. What the hungry need first is bread, and what the frightened need first is safety. Jesus too healed the sick and fed the hungry before he taught. So whoever lives in the age of spiritual striving understands that others are still wrestling with the earlier stages, and never belittles caring for their material needs and their safety. At the same time he does not stop at comfort and knowledge for himself but presses on toward higher meaning. When service that meets our neighbors' needs goes together with the inner striving to find God, both individual lives and society grow together toward light and life.

Because of rebellion and default, Urantia has not been able to follow the order of a normal planet, but the individual can live the age of spiritual striving right here and now. Today, ask yourself whether your faith still rests in fear or is moving forward into the joy of knowing the Father. And do not ignore your heart's thirst for meaning; receive it as an invitation to draw near to God. That very longing for meaning is the voice of the Thought Adjuster within us, calling us higher.
d100.pr: Find and write down one fear that lingers in your faith, and pray that it may be replaced by trust in the Father.

d101.t: Blessed Are Those Who Believe Unseen
msg: Having portrayed the beautiful civilizations of normal worlds ruled by a Planetary Prince, Paper 50 turns in its final section to isolated worlds like Urantia. Through the rebellion of Caligastia our planet lost the visible presence and guidance of a Planetary Prince and a Material Son and Daughter, and it was cut off from the universe circuits as well. On the surface this seems a most unfortunate condition. But today's passage reveals the special opportunity hidden within that misfortune.

The races of isolated worlds are given a unique opportunity for the exercise of faith. It is not easy to believe in God where there are no visible superhuman leaders and no tidings come from on high. For that very reason, the faith that grows here becomes a pure confidence that is not dependent on sight or any other material consideration. The passage calls this a peculiar quality of confidence in cosmic reliability. Hard circumstances actually temper faith and make it strong.

The passage that follows tells us that ascenders from such isolated worlds are called agondonters on Jerusem (see 50:7.2). The name means evolutionary will creatures who can believe without seeing, persevere when isolated, and triumph over insuperable difficulties even when alone. They never lose this identity, even on Paradise, and they are very early intrusted with special cosmic assignments where unquestioned faith and sublime confidence are essential. What seemed to be our weakness becomes an eternal asset.

The words Jesus spoke to Thomas after his resurrection, that blessed are those who have not seen and yet believe, take on a new depth here. We cannot see heavenly beings with our eyes, we cannot confirm at once the answers to our prayers, and often we feel that God is far away. Yet every one of those moments is a lesson in the faith of the agondonter. God has not left us alone; through the indwelling Thought Adjuster and the Spirit of Truth he is always nearest of all.

The Urantia Book makes it clear that this isolation is no eternal curse. Michael chose this very isolated planet as the stage of his final bestowal, and the Spirit of Truth he left behind has been poured out upon all people. So we are never wholly alone. The only difference is that heaven's help comes to us not in visible ways but inwardly. Accepting this changes the posture of our faith. Rather than wandering in search of signs and wonders, we learn to listen to the quiet leading that speaks within. Rather than postponing belief until outward conditions are right, we learn to light a lamp in whatever darkness we are given now. Faith nurtured in this way becomes an inner anchor that does not waver when circumstances change.

If a moment comes today when your heart wavers because God cannot be seen, receive it as the training of an agondonter. Rather than demanding visible proof, remember the love and guidance you have already received, and trust one step further. Faith grown on an isolated planet will one day be used in precious service shining throughout the universe. Remember that each small act of trust today is shaping the agondonter character that will shine in your eternal universe career.
d101.pr: Recall a time when God felt far away, and offer a short prayer confessing your trust even then.

d102.t: A World Visited by Four Sons
msg: Paper 51 explains the mission of the Planetary Adams and Eves, the Material Sons and Daughters of God, on the evolutionary worlds. As biologic uplifters they raise the blood lines of the evolutionary races, and together with the Planetary Prince they serve as the visible leaders of civilization. In the midst of this general account, today's passage suddenly turns to the story of our own world, Urantia. Our planet has been visited by four orders of sonship: Caligastia, the Planetary Prince; Adam and Eve; Machiventa Melchizedek, the sage of Salem; and Christ Michael, who came as the bestowal Son.

This list holds both glory and sorrow. Caligastia joined the Lucifer rebellion and betrayed the planet, and Adam and Eve, through impatience, departed from the plan and failed in their mission. Melchizedek rekindled the dying embers of truth in the days of Abraham, and at last Michael himself came in the flesh. The author of the passage laments how much more effective and beautiful it would have been had Michael been welcomed to our world by a loyal and efficient Planetary Prince and a devoted and successful Material Son. In that lament we sense heaven's deep compassion for the weary road our world has traveled.

Yet this lament does not end in despair. The passage tells us that not all worlds have been so unfortunate as Urantia, and that where the Adams succeed, they contribute to the development of a great people, continuing as the visible heads of planetary affairs even far into the age of light and life. This reminds us that our failure is not the standard of the universe. God's plan was designed from the beginning to unfold in beauty and order, and the confusion on Urantia came not because the plan was wrong but because creature free will was misused. The order of the universe was designed in love, but because love cannot be compelled, it grants freedom, and with that freedom comes the possibility of failure. To read the history of a failed world, therefore, is not to confirm God's impotence but to see the depth of God's patience in so honoring the freedom of his creatures.

At the same time, this passage shows us the remarkable privilege our world holds. Precisely because this planet had suffered so many failures, Michael, sovereign of the universe, chose it as the stage of his final bestowal. Jesus, the Son of Man, lived his earthly life without the help of any visible Planetary Prince or Adam, by faith in and love for the Father alone. His life has therefore become an eternal example showing that God's will can be done wholly even under the hardest conditions (see Paper 120).

This story applies just as much to our personal lives. We too carry a past stained with mistakes and failures, and sometimes we wish we had started out under better conditions. But God does not see our failures as the end. Rather, he is the one who pours out the greatest grace where the deepest wounds are. Just as Urantia became Michael's bestowal planet, the broken places in our lives can become the places where God's love shines most brightly.

Today, call to mind the things in your life that remain as regrets. Then look, in those very places, for traces of the grace God has already given. When we see that God's plan did not stop even behind our failed plans, we can step forward again in gratitude rather than resentment of the past.
d102.pr: Recall one regret in your life, write down one trace of grace that came after it, and give thanks.

d103.t: The Link Between God and Man
msg: The sixth section of Paper 51 explains how the Garden of Eden continues to function as the center of civilization on a normal world. Where the schools of the Planetary Prince teach philosophy, religion, and morality, the garden headquarters of Adam and Eve leads the culture of practical life: agriculture, industry, and home life. Today's passage reveals the deeper meaning of the presence of the Planetary Adam and Eve. In these Material Sons and Daughters we encounter the last and the indispensable link connecting God with man, bridging the almost infinite gulf between the eternal Creator and the lowest finite personalities of time.

This expression shows how tenderly the Universal Father draws near to his children. God is infinite and we are finite. The distance between is one we could never cross by our own strength. And so God sends many orders of sons and spirits to bridge that gulf step by step. The Planetary Prince and his staff are invisible to mortal eyes, but the Material Sons and Daughters, though physical and even sex creatures like us, are able to see and comprehend the invisible spirit beings. They are interpreters and guides between the visible and invisible worlds.

On Urantia, because of the default of Adam and Eve, this link was never able to function fully. We inherited part of the blood line they left behind, but we did not enjoy the blessing of having them beside us over long ages, interpreting the Planetary Prince to us and showing us the order of heaven. This lack is one of the reasons our civilization has had such difficulty holding on to spiritual values. Yet knowing of this loss, rather than discouraging us, makes us treasure all the more the channels of connection given to us now. When we honestly acknowledge this lack, we understand why faith demands such great effort in this world. To believe in what is unseen, and to discern the order of heaven without a guide to explain it, is never easy. But because we know how hard it is, we can look more generously upon one another's journeys of faith.

We have no visible Adam now, but we have a more direct connection. The indwelling Thought Adjuster, a fragment of the Father, dwells within our minds, and the Spirit of Truth poured out by Michael is present in the hearts of all people. And the life of Jesus has become the most perfect link of all, showing in human words and deeds what God is like. In him we have come to see and understand the invisible Father (see Paper 169).

This passage also leads us to consider that each of us can become a small link for others. Just as Adam and Eve interpreted the invisible Prince to mortals, those who know God can show the love of the invisible God to their neighbors through their own lives. A kind word, an honest deed, a patient heart can be the most convincing evidence to someone else that God is real. Faith is passed on more deeply when it is seen in a life than when it is explained in words.

Today, try living as a bridge between God and people. Do not keep the comfort and peace you have received from God locked within yourself; pass them on to someone who needs them. When we do so, we become people who carry on, in however small a way, the lost mission of Eden.
d103.pr: Decide on one small kindness that will show God's love to someone you meet today, and do it.

msg: Paper 52 surveys the stages through which humanity on a normal evolutionary world grows, from primitive times to the age of light and life. In describing the first stage, primitive man, today's passage declares a vital truth: all mortals who are indwelt by Thought Adjusters are potential worshipers. They have been lighted by the true light, and they possess capacity for seeking reciprocal contact with divinity. This means that no one is excluded from the capacity to seek God.

But the passage does not hide reality. The early religion of primitive man is largely a persistence of animal fear coupled with ignorant awe and tribal superstition. People feared thunder and lightning, sought to appease invisible ghosts, and tried to control what they could not understand by magic. The Urantia Book frankly points out that the survival of superstition to this day is hardly complimentary to our evolutionary development nor compatible with our otherwise splendid achievements in material progress. Even in an age of advanced science and technology, religious habits founded on fear still hold the minds of many.

Nevertheless, the passage does not simply disparage this primitive religion. This early fear religion served a very valuable purpose in subduing the fiery tempers of these primitive creatures. It was the forerunner of civilization and the soil for the subsequent planting of the seeds of revealed religion by the Planetary Prince and his ministers. God works according to the level of humanity, using even immature religion as a preparation for receiving higher truth. That evolutionary religion and revealed religion together lead humanity forward is a teaching running through the whole of The Urantia Book (see Paper 92). Our personal journeys of faith unfold in much the same way. Childhood faith often begins with fear of punishment or hope of reward. That is nothing to be ashamed of. What matters is not to remain there but to grow into a faith of love and trust. God does not blame us for our immature starting point; he waits patiently for us to grow.

Seen in the light of our personal lives, this passage brings both great comfort and a challenge. The comfort is that each of us has already been lighted by the true light. The Thought Adjuster within me was leading me toward God even before I knew God. If I feel a desire to worship, a longing for something greater and better, that is a sign that the worshiper's nature planted within me is awakening. The capacity to seek God is not given only to a special few.

The challenge is to examine honestly the primitive elements still lingering in our faith. Do I worship because I love God, or am I appeasing a deity to avoid punishment and win blessing? Is my prayer fellowship with the Father, or an incantation for getting what I want? The religion Jesus revealed was founded not on fear but on love. He revealed God not as a terrifying judge but as a loving Father.

Today, offer your worship not as a duty or a bargain but as a response of love. Take even a short time to ask for nothing at all, simply giving thanks as you contemplate who the Father is. In that moment we grow one step further beyond primitive fear toward becoming true worshipers.
d104.pr: Spend five minutes in worship, asking for nothing, simply giving thanks as you contemplate who God is.

msg: The sixth section of Paper 52 deals with Urantia's post-bestowal age. On a normal world the coming of a bestowal Son opens an era of world-wide peace, but because of rebellion and Adam's default our world has not followed that order. How, then, can the brotherhood of man be realized on Urantia? After treating in turn racial purification, intellectual cross-fertilization, ethical awakening, and political wisdom, the section offers as its fifth factor today's passage, spiritual insight. And it says that this is the quickest way.

The first sentence of the passage lays the foundation for the whole discussion: the brotherhood of man is, after all, predicated on the recognition of the fatherhood of God. We are brothers and sisters not because we share a nation or a race but because we share the same Father. Without knowing God as Father, brotherhood easily remains mere sentiment or slogan. But when we truly realize that God is the Father of all people, strangers become our brothers, and even enemies begin to appear as the Father's children. The heart of the gospel Jesus taught was likewise the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man. Most human conflict arises when we forget the source that binds us together and see one another only as rivals or threats. But the moment we remember our one Father, differences begin to appear not as threats but as a rich diversity.

The passage says that the only technique for accelerating the natural trend of social evolution is that of applying spiritual pressure from above. Institutions and laws, education and economic reform are all needed, but by themselves they cannot fundamentally change the human heart. Spiritual pressure does two things at once. It augments moral insight, and it enhances the soul capacity of every mortal to understand and love every other mortal. Only when the power to discern right from wrong and the power to embrace others grow together does brotherhood become reality.

The words to notice here are mutual understanding and fraternal love. The passage calls these transcendent civilizers. Love without understanding easily collapses into misunderstanding, and understanding without love remains cold analysis. When the sincere effort to understand another's situation and thoughts goes together with warmly accepting the person so understood, the world changes little by little. The Urantia Book sees this as something that begins with the spiritual transformation of each individual.

World peace and the brotherhood of mankind, then, begin in my own heart before they are vast political projects. The more deeply I know God as Father, the more my capacity grows to treat my neighbor as a brother. When I take one step toward understanding someone I dislike, I am actually taking a step toward the brotherhood of man. One small reconciliation, one prejudice laid down, becomes part of the spiritual pressure that changes the world (see Paper 194).

Today, think of one person who differs from you in outlook or with whom your relationship is uncomfortable. Remembering that he or she is also a child of the same Father, try looking at the situation once from that person's point of view. That small effort to understand may be the key that opens the door to brotherhood.
d105.pr: Think of someone with whom your relationship is uneasy as a child of the same Father, and consider the situation once from their point of view.

msg: Paper 53 records how Lucifer, sovereign of the local system of Satania, came to rebel. He was a being of brilliant ability and dazzling personality, a leader trusted by multitudes. To the question of how such a one could fall, today's passage gives a clear answer: no one ever suggested rebellion to Lucifer. The idea of self-assertion in opposition to the will of Michael and to the plans of the Universal Father had its origin in his own mind.

This fact gives deep insight into the origin of evil. We usually look outside ourselves for the causes of wrongdoing. We say someone egged us on, circumstances drove us to it, the temptation was too strong. External influences are certainly real. But the story of Lucifer shows that the most fundamental rebellion can grow within one's own mind with no outside temptation at all. The seeds are the thought of exalting oneself, the pride of believing one knows better, the reluctance to be governed by another.

The passage tells us that Lucifer's relations with the Creator Son had been intimate and always cordial. The rebellion did not erupt suddenly out of a cold and hostile relationship. Even within a relationship of love and trust, cracks slowly formed once his own mind began to exalt itself. For a long time he did not voice his dissatisfaction, yet for more than one hundred years of standard time the Union of Days sensed and reported that all was not at peace in Lucifer's mind. Outwardly he was quiet, but within, discontent was growing. This record also shows how long the administration of heaven is willing to wait in patience. Even while unrest grew in Lucifer's mind, the rulers of the universe did not intervene by force but gave him the chance to turn back of his own accord. Because God respects the freedom of the mind, he keeps the door of repentance open to the very end. Whether or not we walk through that door is always our own choice.

This passage teaches us how important it is to watch over the peace of our minds. Great wrongs do not happen overnight. Small complaints, unresolved resentments, and self-justified self-pity pile up over a long time until one day they break out in action. A loss of inner peace is a signal that something needs to be set right. At such times we should honestly lay that heart open before God, and if necessary confide in someone we trust. Lucifer nursed his discontent in secret, and in the end he fell, dragging multitudes down with him (see Paper 54).

The Urantia Book clearly distinguishes self-respect from self-assertion. To value oneself as a child of God is healthy. But self-assertion that puts the self at the center of the universe and rejects all order and authority leads to ruin. Jesus walked the opposite road. Though he was sovereign of the universe, he prayed, not my will but yours be done. True greatness comes not from exalting oneself but from obeying in love.

Today, examine whether some complaint or resentment has long been lingering in your heart. However small it may seem, do not leave it there; lay it before God in prayer. Tending early to a heart that has lost its peace is the surest way to prevent a great fall.
d106.pr: Find one complaint you have long harbored, lay it before God in prayer, and ask for peace.

msg: The eighth section of Paper 53 tells how Jesus, the Son of Man, came to Urantia and confronted the forces of the Lucifer rebellion. On the mount of temptation he rejected the enticements of Caligastia, and through the cross and the resurrection he greatly broke the influence of the rebels over this world. Today's passage shows what that victory means for each of our lives: no fallen spirit ever did have the power to invade the minds or to harass the souls of the children of God.

This is great news of liberation. Throughout history many people have lived in the grip of the fear of evil spirits. The dread that unseen evil forces could seize them at any moment gave rise to countless superstitions and magical practices. But The Urantia Book declares that neither Satan nor Caligastia could ever touch or approach the faith sons of God. The words, He who is born of God keeps himself, and the wicked one touches him not, are literally true.

The key sentence of the passage is the declaration that faith is an effective armor against sin and iniquity. Armor turns aside attacks coming from without. A heart that trusts God, a sincere longing to do the Father's will, becomes a shield no outside force can pierce. This protection does not come from special rituals or incantations but from a living relationship with God. As long as we trust him, our souls are safe in his hands. Faith is not a matter of the strength of our feelings but of their direction. Even on days when faith feels weak, if we have only the small will to turn our hearts toward God, that armor still surrounds us. God looks not at our wavering emotions but at the direction in which our hearts are turned. So rather than losing heart because our faith is weak, it is enough to turn our hearts toward him once again today.

The passage that follows adds another honest truth. When weak and dissolute mortals are supposed to be under the influence of devils and demons, they are merely being dominated by their own inherent and debased tendencies. The devil has been given a great deal of credit for evil which does not belong to him. These words hand responsibility back to us. Blaming the devil when we do wrong is an easy excuse, but true growth begins with honestly acknowledging the animal tendencies and selfish habits within ourselves.

This passage, then, frees us from fear and at the same time sets us face to face with responsibility. We need not fear unseen evil forces. But we must stay awake to our own weaknesses and wrong tendencies. And the power to overcome those weaknesses also comes from faith. The indwelling Thought Adjuster and the Spirit of Truth help us every day to make better choices, and faith is the very channel through which we receive that help (see Paper 149).

Today, when fear comes or temptation draws near, remember that you are wearing the armor of faith. And when you stumble, rather than blaming others or evil forces, honestly own your part and take hold of God's hand again. That honesty and trust guard us more securely than anything else.
d107.pr: Whenever fear arises today, recall the truth that whoever is born of God is safe, and offer a prayer of trust.

msg: In dealing with the many problems left by the Lucifer rebellion, Paper 54 first asks about the nature of liberty. Lucifer raised the cry of liberty as he launched his rebellion. He claimed that breaking free of the order and supervision of the universe was true emancipation. But the result was not emancipation; it was confusion and ruin for multitudes of beings. Today's passage pinpoints the root of this tragedy: unbridled self-will and unregulated self-expression equal unmitigated selfishness, the acme of ungodliness.

The passage overturns what we commonly think about freedom. We easily take freedom to mean being able to do whatever we like. But The Urantia Book says that liberty without the associated and ever-increasing conquest of self is a figment of egoistic mortal imagination. Self-motivated liberty is a conceptual illusion, a cruel deception. License masquerading in the garments of liberty is the forerunner of abject bondage. Those who live by their desires seem free at first, but in time they become slaves to those very desires. True freedom is not the absence of outward restraint but release from the impulses that drive us from within. The freest person of all is the one who is not dragged along by anger, not swayed by greed, and not ruled by fear.

The passage goes on to set true and false liberty side by side. True liberty is the associate of genuine self-respect; false liberty is the consort of self-admiration. True liberty is the fruit of self-control; false liberty, the assumption of self-assertion. This contrast is finely drawn. Self-respect and self-admiration look alike on the surface, but they point in entirely different directions. Self-respect, knowing its dignity as a child of God, governs itself; self-admiration uses others to exalt itself.

The last sentence of the passage shows where the two roads end. Self-control leads to altruistic service; self-admiration tends towards the exploitation of others. Those who know how to govern themselves spend their surplus strength serving others. Those bent on exalting themselves, on the other hand, seek to lord it over others even at the cost of righteous attainment. Lucifer walked the latter road; Jesus walked the former. He possessed all power, yet he used it not for himself but for service (see Paper 136).

This teaching poses concrete questions for our daily lives. What am I justifying in the name of freedom? Behind my wish to have my own way, is consideration for others missing? True freedom is not being bound to nothing, but being gladly bound to love and truth. That we taste the deepest freedom precisely when we freely obey the will of God is an ancient paradox of faith and a truth of the universe. Self-control does not diminish freedom; it is the fence that protects it.

Today, examine in one particular situation whether the freedom you enjoy is true liberty or false. Instead of saying everything you want to say, hold back once; instead of taking at once what you desire, think first of someone else. That small act of self-control will free you from the bondage of desire and lead you into the joy of service.
d108.pr: Pause once today before a word or action you want to indulge, and fill that space with consideration for someone else.

msg: Many who read Paper 54 carry the same question. Why did the rulers of the universe not crush Lucifer's rebellion at once? Why is evil permitted for so long? This paper answers that question in two sections, on the time lag of justice and the mercy time lag. Today's passage contains the heart of the answer: supreme justice can act instantly when not restrained by divine mercy, but the ministry of mercy always provides a saving interval between seedtime and harvest.

This interval works in two directions. If the seed sowing is good, the time of waiting provides for the testing and upbuilding of character. In the time when we do good yet receive no immediate reward, we learn patience and faithfulness. If the seed sowing is evil, this merciful delay provides time for repentance and rectification. That judgment does not fall at once when we do wrong is not because God is indifferent, but because he is giving us the chance to turn back. Just as a farmer does not harvest the moment he sows, the spiritual life too has its seasons of waiting. Enduring those seasons, we learn to value the process above the result and faithfulness above reward. Waiting is not wasted time; it is the time when roots grow deep.

The passage says that this time delay in the adjudication and execution of evildoers is inherent in the mercy ministry of the seven superuniverses. It is not an incidental leniency but a fundamental principle of the universe. And that principle proves one thing: this restraint of justice by mercy proves that God is love, and that such a God of love dominates the universes and in mercy controls the fate and judgment of all his creatures. The government of the universe is not the cold enforcement of law but a rule led by love.

This truth rebukes our impatience. When we see injustice we want punishment to fall at once, and when we do good we want reward to follow at once. But God's time is not our time. Even if evil seems to flourish for long, it is not that justice has vanished but that mercy is waiting. The passage that follows adds that even this merciful delay does not go on forever (see 54:4.8). Opportunity is given generously, but it is not unlimited.

At the same time, this truth applies to us. I too have done countless wrongs, yet I have lived to this day without being judged at once. That is not because I was right, but because God's mercy waited for me. If so, I too must show the same mercy to others. Not condemning at once those who wrong me, but giving them time to turn back, is to resemble God's own rule. This is exactly what Jesus taught when he told us to forgive even seventy times seven.

Today, if you have lost heart because you did good and saw no fruit, receive this as a time for building character. And if there is a wrong you have not yet set right, do not put off this time that mercy has given you; use it for repentance and rectification. The time between seedtime and harvest is the most precious grace we have been given.
d109.pr: Find one wrong you have not yet set right, and begin an apology or correction today, within the time mercy has given.

msg: Paper 55 portrays a world settled in light and life, the highest state an evolutionary planet can attain. On such a world a morontia temple is built at the capital, and there something remarkable takes place. Mortals who have grown sufficiently in spirit are translated to the morontia state by fusion with their Thought Adjusters, without passing through natural death. While family and friends look on, they vanish in the flash of fusion and awaken on the mansion worlds. Today's passage describes the hearts of those gathered around that scene.

The souls of these progressing mortals are increasingly filled with faith, hope, and assurance. And the mood of those gathered around the translation shrine is not sorrow but joy. The passage likens it to the spirit of joyful friends and relatives who might assemble at a graduating exercise for one of their group, or who might come together to witness the conferring of some great honor upon one of their number. Everyone knows that this parting is not an end but a promotion to be celebrated. For them, leaving this world means going up to the next school.

The last sentence of the passage is counsel addressed to us: it would be decidedly helpful if less advanced mortals could only learn to view natural death with something of this same cheerfulness and lightheartedness. We who live on Urantia have not yet experienced fusion translation; we must pass through physical death. But only the manner of death differs; the reality beyond it is the same. For a God-knowing soul, death is the doorway into the mansion worlds, and beyond that door life continues without a break. Such celebration is not a forced concealment of grief. It is a peace that wells up naturally from a deep knowledge of how things truly are in the universe. Because they know where the departing one is going, who will welcome him, and when they will meet again, they can smile even at a parting. Knowledge drives out fear.

In our culture death is the greatest fear and the greatest taboo. We shrink from speaking of it, and we despair in its presence. Of course the grief of losing someone we love is a natural and honest emotion; Jesus himself wept at the tomb of Lazarus. But beneath that grief, hope and assurance can flow. The Urantia Book tells us in detail that survival is no vague hope but an intricate plan of the universe, and that teachers and companions await us on the mansion worlds (see Paper 47).

To look upon death as a graduation also changes how we live today. A student about to graduate does not waste the time that remains but tries faithfully to learn what must be learned. In the same way, those who see life on earth as a school devote themselves every day to learning love, seeking truth, and refining character. Those freed from the fear of death come, if anything, to love life more deeply. Knowing that they will one day depart, they become kinder to those they meet today and more faithful in today's work.

Today, quietly reflect on your own thoughts about death. If they are filled only with fear and despair, lay God's promises over them. And live this day as a day of faithful learning, so that you may one day greet your own graduation with joy.
d110.pr: Picture death as a graduation to the next school, and write down one thing you most want to learn before you graduate.

msg: The sixth section of Paper 55 portrays the life of the individual mortal in the age of light and life. Even on such a world, people are still born in bodies, and they learn, work, and love. What, then, has changed? Today's passage says that the difference lies above all in inner spiritual communion. The Adjusters continue to come as in former evolutionary eras, and as the epochs pass, these mortals are increasingly able to commune with the indwelling Father fragment.

This gives us great hope. The Thought Adjuster received by those who live on worlds of light and life is in essence the same fragment of the Father as the Adjuster within us. The difference lies not in the gift but in the degree of cooperation with that gift. Helped by generations of education and culture and a spiritual environment, they have come to commune more deeply with the Adjuster. If so, we too can deepen that communion right here and now. Our surroundings are less favorable, but the possibility is open to us just the same. A deepening communion means not only growing knowledge of God but a growing intimacy with God. It is moving from knowing the Father only with the head to keeping company with him in the heart. This intimacy does not come overnight; it grows through small daily responses and acts of obedience.

The passage also tells us that many heavenly ministries work together. The adjutant mind-spirits are still functioning, and the Holy Spirit and the ministry of angels are even more effective as the successive epochs of settled life are experienced. In the fourth stage, advanced mortals seem to experience considerable conscious contact with the spirit presence of the Master Spirit of superuniverse jurisdiction. And the philosophy of such a world is focused upon the attempt to comprehend the new revelations of God the Supreme. Spiritual progress is not achieved alone; it is accomplished by the cooperation of countless ministries of the universe.

On these advanced worlds, more than one half of the inhabitants experience translation to the morontia state from among the living. That means that so many have deepened their communion with the Adjuster until at last they attain fusion. The passage sums up all these changes in the words, old things are passing away; behold, all things are becoming new. This is no distant dream but a reality already being realized throughout the universe, and a promise that will one day be fulfilled on Urantia as well (see 55:7.3).

What, then, can we do today? The way to deepen communion with the Adjuster is not some special secret but steady spiritual habit. Times of quietly worshiping God, times of honestly examining ourselves, and sincere prayer seeking the Father's will widen that channel. The Urantia Book teaches that the Adjuster works through our highest thoughts and ideals (see Paper 110). Every choice to love truth and choose goodness deepens our inner communion one step further.

Today, pause for a moment during the day and become aware of the fragment of the Father within you. You need not use words. Acknowledge that he is there, and quietly offer him your desire to follow his will. Those brief moments of communion will accumulate and one day lead us to eternal fusion. Small moments of communion gather into an eternal friendship.
d111.pr: Pause three times today to become aware of the Thought Adjuster within you, and affirm that you will follow his will.

msg: Paper 56 is a majestic paper on universal unity. It shows that physical creation, the intellectual realm, spiritual reality, personality, and Deity itself are all woven into one. Its eighth section introduces the Supreme Being as the supreme unifier. The Supreme is the experiential Deity who grows together with the evolving universes of time and space, and who is also being actualized in the experience of mortals. Today's passage describes our relationship with this Supreme Being in very practical terms.

The passage begins with the words, bear in mind. All that God the Father and his Paradise Sons do for us, we in turn and in spirit have the opportunity to do for and in the emerging Supreme Being. We are not beings who only receive. By passing on to others the love and care we receive from God, we too take part in the growth of the universe. Each small good deed of ours adds to the actualization of the evolving Supreme Being.

The second sentence of the passage sums up a principle of the universe in a few words: the experience of love, joy, and service in the universe is mutual. Love is not a one-way street. Love received is completed when it is given again, joy shared grows greater, and service begets service. The universe lives, moves, and grows through such a circulation. A life that only receives and never passes on stagnates like still water, but a life that shares what it receives spreads life like a flowing river. Those who are loved learn how to love, and those who are comforted become able to comfort others. Every gift we have received was given not to stop with us but to flow farther through us.

The last sentence of the passage holds an especially deep insight. God the Father does not need that his sons should return to him all that he bestows upon them. God needs nothing, and he does not ask us to repay him. Instead, his sons in turn bestow all of this upon their fellows and upon the evolving Supreme Being. The best way to repay the grace we receive from God is not so much to offer something directly to him as to extend that grace to our neighbors.

This teaching is deeply in tune with the words of Jesus: inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these my brethren, you did it to me. The way of loving God is not separate from the way of loving people. The Urantia Book teaches the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man together, and says that the Father's love we have received is completed only when it flows out in service to our brothers (see Paper 103). Grace is not wealth to be hoarded but a stream to be passed along.

Today, count one by one the graces you have received from God. There will be life itself, the people you love, the joy of coming to know truth, the help you received in times of crisis. Then choose one of them and extend it in the same form to someone else. When we do, we take part in the growth of the Supreme Being within the universe's circulation of love. When the love we have received flows on, our lives grow wider too.
d112.pr: Choose one grace you have received from God and give a gift of the same kind to one other person today.

msg: The last section of Paper 56 deals with three divine values: truth, beauty, and goodness. On worlds settled in light and life, people come to understand God more deeply through these three values. Philosophy explores truth, art pursues beauty, and religion holds fast to goodness. Yet these three are not separate; they are lights shining from different angles on one divinity reality. Today's passage beautifully shows where these three values lead.

The passage first says that to finite man truth, beauty, and goodness embrace the full revelation of divinity reality. We cannot see God directly, but we experience him when we meet what is true, when we behold what is beautiful, when we do what is good. In the moment a scientist discovers a law of nature, the moment an artist brings forth harmony, the moment someone gives himself for a neighbor, God is near us in every such moment. The ways of meeting God in everyday life are open this widely.

The passage goes on to say that as this love-comprehension of Deity finds spiritual expression in the lives of God-knowing mortals, there are yielded the fruits of divinity: intellectual peace, social progress, moral satisfaction, spiritual joy, and cosmic wisdom. Savoring these five fruits one by one, we see that faith never stays in one corner of life. Faith brings peace to our thinking, advances society, satisfies conscience, gladdens the soul, and gives wisdom to understand the universe. The principle Jesus spoke of, that a tree is known by its fruits, applies here exactly. The genuineness of faith is shown not in words or rituals but in such fruits. It is a good test to ask whether my faith is making me more peaceful, more honest, and more joyful.

The last sentence of the passage is the conclusion of this whole paper and the heart of The Urantia Book as a whole. The advanced mortals on a world in the seventh stage of light and life have learned that love is the greatest thing in the universe, and they know that God is love. The majestic discussion of universal unity gathers at last into this simple truth. At the end of all the explanations of energy and gravity, mind and spirit, the Supreme and the Ultimate, what we meet is God who is love (see Paper 2).

This truth gives us both humility and courage. Humility means acknowledging that we cannot understand all the mysteries of the universe. Courage is the assurance that, even so, we can already know what matters most. Whoever knows that God is love, and that love is the greatest thing, will never be lost in the universe. Even without mastering complex doctrines or deep philosophies, those who learn and practice love day by day already hold what the people of worlds settled in light and life have learned over long ages.

Today, live the day with eyes of truth, beauty, and goodness. Learn one true thing, enjoy one beautiful thing, and do one good thing. Then give thanks to the God of love who stands behind them all. May this be a day on which your own life confirms the truth that love is the greatest thing.
d113.pr: Learn one true thing, enjoy one beautiful thing, and do one good thing, then offer a prayer of thanks.

msg: Paper 57 tells the story of Urantia's origin on the basis of the records of Jerusem. The story begins in an almost unimaginably remote past, about nine hundred billion years ago. Today's passage sums up the starting point of that long story in a single sentence: Urantia is of origin in our sun, and our sun is one of the multifarious offspring of the Andronover nebula, which was onetime organized as a component part of the physical power and material matter of the local universe of Nebadon. And this great nebula itself took origin in the universal force-charge of space in the superuniverse of Orvonton, long, long ago.

This short sentence contains the cosmic genealogy of where our home came from. The ground we stand on, the water we drink, the elements that make up our bodies, all came from a flow of energy that began in space hundreds of billions of years ago. That energy became a nebula, the nebula gave birth to countless suns, and from one of those suns our planet was born. We are not beings set apart from the universe but the product of its long, long history. Knowing this, the stars in the night sky feel less like strangers and more like distant relatives.

The Urantia Book teaches that this whole process took place not by chance but under plan and supervision. The earlier part of this paper explains that the Paradise force organizers mobilized the forces of space to initiate the nebula, and that the universe power directors followed after them to control its energies (see 57:1.4). The physical universe is not an indifferent machine but the stage on which the will of the Universal Father unfolds. Behind the majestic physical process of a nebula turning and suns being born, there was a mind of love and purpose.

This cosmic perspective gives two gifts to our daily lives. The first is humility. Before hundreds of billions of years and immeasurable space, how small our worries and quarrels are! The problem troubling me today is, in the time of the universe, a passing moment. The second is dignity. That life appeared after such long preparation, and that at last there emerged human beings capable of knowing God, is evidence that our existence is by no means trivial. The universe has waited long ages to welcome us. My being born here is the fruit of the universe's long waiting, and within that waiting lies the Creator's deep hope for us. So we have no reason to sink into futility, regarding ourselves as products of chance.

The origin of the universe as uncovered by science and creation as confessed by faith do not oppose each other. The Urantia Book respects physical fact while helping us see the meaning beyond it. To know how the stars came to be is science; to ask why they came to be is philosophy; and to know that all of it came from a God of love is religion. When these three are in harmony, we understand the universe more fully. The wonder we feel gazing at the stars can be the first step of worship.

If you have the chance tonight to look up at the sky, remember that those stars and we ourselves came from the same source. And give thanks to the Universal Father who planned it all and has waited so long. That I am alive and breathing today, within the long history of the universe, is itself a wondrous gift.
d114.pr: Gaze at the night sky or the sunlight, and take time to give thanks for your life, given after hundreds of billions of years of preparation.

d115.t: The Council That Planned for Life
msg: The last section of Paper 57 covers the era when the crust was stabilizing and the oceans were forming. As Urantia was being made ready to receive life, another preparation was under way on high. Today's passage records that process in plain terms. Arrangements for the planetary occupation were completed by the mixed commission of twelve on Jerusem and approved by the planetary commission of seventy on Edentia, and these plans, proposed by the advisory counselors of the Life Carriers, were finally accepted on Salvington.

This brief record shows that life never began by chance. Planting life on a planet was something carefully examined and approved through many levels, the local system, the constellation, and the local universe. Jerusem, Edentia, and Salvington, the headquarters of system, constellation, and universe, all took part in this decision. The life we now enjoy is the result of long deliberation and cooperation among many wise beings. Knowing this, we feel afresh how precious each life is. When we picture the many discussions and judgments that passed through those commissions, we can sense with what careful love life was prepared. The administration of heaven does not decide carelessly; it always works through wisdom, consultation, and approval. This is a good example for the way our own communities make decisions, too.

The passage goes on to tell that soon thereafter the Nebadon broadcasts carried the announcement that Urantia would become the stage of the sixtieth Satania experiment. Our planet was designated a life-modification world, designed by the Life Carriers to amplify and improve the Satania type of the Nebadon life patterns. The next paper explains that there are only sixty-one such worlds in all of Satania (see 58:0.1). From the very beginning, Urantia was a planet holding a special experiment and special hopes.

This fact lets us see the hardships of our planet with new eyes. To be an experimental planet means greater possibilities along with greater uncertainty. Compared with a world following a fixed pattern, there are more variations and challenges, and so also more trial and error. The rebellion and default Urantia has suffered, and its biologic confusion, are in some ways bound up with this character. But precisely because it was such a world, Michael chose it as the stage of his bestowal, and the faith grown here has acquired an unusual strength.

This passage applies to our personal lives as well. Each of our lives also began under heaven's careful attention. The Thought Adjuster comes from Paradise for each one of us and dwells in our minds, and guardian angels and many spirit beings help us grow. Even if my life seems ordinary and full of failure, it is an experiment and adventure that heaven watches with hope. A life that grows by its own choices is harder than one that follows a fixed pattern, but it bears fruit that is all the more precious.

Today, remember that your life has been built on the love and cooperation of many. Parents and teachers, friends, and the unseen ministers of heaven have worked for your life. Give thanks to them, and resolve to become a fellow worker who helps the lives of others. Life is always something we accomplish together.
d115.pr: Think of three people who have helped shape your life, and speak a word of thanks to one of them.

msg: Paper 58 tells, in the voice of a Life Carrier, how life was established on Urantia. The Life Carriers are Sons of the local universe who, at the direction of the Creator Son and the Mother Spirit, plant life on the planets and watch over its evolution. Today's passage begins by correcting a common misunderstanding of their name. We can and do carry life to the planets, the Life Carrier says, but we brought no life to Urantia.

According to the passage, Urantia life is unique, original with the planet. This sphere is a life-modification world; all life appearing hereon was formulated by the Life Carriers right here on the planet. It was not life already made elsewhere and transplanted, but life freshly shaped within the seas and chemical conditions of this earth. And there is no other world in all Satania, even in all Nebadon, that has a life existence just like that of Urantia. The life of our planet is a work of which there is only one in the universe.

This fact awakens us anew to the worth of the world we live in. From forests and rivers, birds and fish, all the way to human beings, all life on this earth takes forms found nowhere else in the universe in quite the same way. The Life Carriers tended this life with care for long ages, and from it at last emerged human beings endowed with will. When we treat nature carelessly, we are damaging a work that exists only once in the universe. A heart that respects life is bound up with a heart that respects the will of the Creator. When the Life Carriers shaped life in the seas of this earth, they strove to find forms exactly suited to this planet's conditions. That devoted care remains intact in the remarkable balance of the ecosystem we enjoy today.

This passage also leads us to reflect on our own uniqueness. Just as Urantia life is like that of no other world, each of our personalities is one of a kind in the universe. The Urantia Book teaches that personality is a gift bestowed directly by the Universal Father, and that no two personalities are ever alike (see Paper 112). So there is no need to sink into feelings of inferiority by comparing ourselves with others, or to strain to become like someone else. God loves me as myself, and wants me to grow in my own unique way.

At the same time, being unique does not mean being isolated. Urantia life is unique, yet it was shaped within the larger order of the Nebadon life patterns. In the same way, our unique personalities find their meaning within the great community of God's family. Many different uniquenesses coming together to form a richer whole: that is the beauty of the universe. As much as we cherish our own uniqueness, we must respect the uniqueness of others. Differences are not threats but evidence of how rich God's creation is.

Today, look at the life around you with new eyes. A single blade of grass by the road, a single bird outside the window, is life of this earth found nowhere else in the universe. And remember that the person in the mirror is also a unique personality whom God has shaped only once. Give thanks for that uniqueness, and resolve to use it beautifully for God and your neighbor.
d116.pr: Look for a long moment at one living thing near you, and give thanks for the life of this earth, found nowhere else in the universe.

d117.t: A Story Written in the Stone Book
msg: The last section of Paper 58 opens the book of geologic history. In the rocks of the life-dawn era the traces of early life remain as fossils, and above them, age by age, the records of new life are laid down layer upon layer. Today's passage says that all of this story is graphically told within the fossil pages of the vast stone book of world record. And it adds that the pages of this gigantic biogeologic record unfailingly tell the truth if you but acquire skill in their interpretation.

This expression offers a beautiful way of seeing nature as a book. The strata beneath the ground are not heaps of soil piled up by chance but a chronicle of life recorded over hundreds of millions of years. Many of these ancient sea beds are now elevated high upon land, and their deposits tell the story of the life struggles of those early days. The rock we tread on as we climb a mountain was once the bottom of the sea, and within it the traces of countless lives lie sleeping. As the poet the passage quotes has said, it is literally true that the dust we tread upon was once alive. Each fossil is the testimony of a life that once received the sunlight, breathed, and lived. The struggles and adaptations of those small lives, accumulating over and over, became the foundation of the world we live in today. We stand, as it were, upon the labors of innumerable lives. This humbles us and makes us cherish all the more the living things on this earth now.

What is especially worth noting in the passage is the condition, if you but acquire skill in their interpretation. The stone book tells the truth, but reading it requires honest and diligent inquiry. Read with prejudice, it leads to mistaken conclusions; followed humbly, fact by fact, it brings us near the truth. The Urantia Book respects the honest inquiry of science and teaches that true science and true religion never conflict (see Paper 103). For the book of nature and the book of revelation come from the same Author.

This perspective gives us a new sense of time. A single page of the stone book took millions of years to lay down. For life to advance from simple forms to complex ones required unimaginably long ages. God is not in a hurry. His creation proceeds patiently, slowly, but surely. So it is with our spiritual growth. Rather than hoping to become perfect overnight, we should treasure the pages of growth written one line at a time, day by day.

This passage also reminds us that our own lives are a book. The choices we make and the deeds we do do not vanish; they remain in our character and in the records of the universe. The Urantia Book tells us that there are recorders on high who preserve the facts of the universe. What story, then, does the page of life I am writing today contain? Let us live so that when someone reads that page in days to come, they will find the marks of love and faithfulness.

Today, look for a moment at the ground beneath your feet or the rocks around you, and recall the long story of life contained within them. Then, giving thanks for God's patient creation, write the page of your today with care. Line by line, it will become a story that remains for eternity.
d117.pr: Choose one sentence you want to leave on the page of your life today, and live the day by that sentence.

d118.t: All Life Leans on Other Life
msg: Paper 59 records the marine-life era of Urantia period by period. It is a long history in which trilobites flourished in the shallow seas, continents sank and rose again and again, and a great variety of marine life appeared and passed away. Today's passage deals with the first great continental flood stage. This was the great age of individual animal organismal evolution, and the marine fauna developed to the point where every type of life below the vertebrate scale was represented in the fossils of those rocks which were laid down during these times.

But the passage tells us that even amid this abundance there were clear limits. All of these animals were marine organisms. No land animals had yet appeared except a few types of worms which burrowed along the seashores, nor had the land plants yet overspread the continents. There was still too much carbon dioxide in the air to permit of the existence of air breathers. Life could advance only as far as the way had been prepared, and it had to wait for its environment to ripen. Here too the unhurried order of creation is revealed. This waiting was not wasted. In the sea, life tried out many forms and gathered strength for the next stage. When the environment was ready, life could move onto the land without delay. Times of preparation always hasten the time of the leap.

The last sentence of the passage states a principle that applies beyond this era to all life. Primarily, all animals except certain of the more primitive ones are directly or indirectly dependent on plant life for their existence. Animals cannot make nourishment from sunlight by themselves. They eat the life energy that plants have made from the light, or obtain it through other animals that have eaten plants. Human beings are no exception. Every food we eat begins, in the end, with plants that grew in the sunlight.

This simple biological fact holds a deep spiritual lesson. No life exists alone. All life lives by leaning on other life, and the chain of dependence leads at last to a single source. As Paper 56 says, the universe is one whole, and no being lives in isolation (see 56:10.14). We lean on nature, we lean on our neighbors, and ultimately we lean on the Universal Father, the source of all life. Dependence is not weakness; it is the very nature of life.

When we accept this truth, gratitude and responsibility grow together. Gratitude comes from knowing that everything I enjoy has come from the labor and sacrifice of other lives. Even a single meal contains sunlight, soil, and rain, the farmer's sweat, and the contributions of countless living things. Responsibility comes from the fact that I too am someone others lean on. When I use the life energy I have received to sustain others, I keep my rightful place in the chain of life. A life of leaning on and helping one another, rather than boasting of self-sufficiency, is a life in keeping with the order of the universe.

When you eat today, pause a moment and recall the countless lives the food has depended on to reach you. Then give thanks to God who sustains all life, and resolve that you too will be someone others can lean on. A life of mutual dependence is the very way of life.
d118.pr: Before eating, recall the living things and people who helped bring the food to you, and offer a prayer of thanks.

d119.t: The Cradle That Fulfilled Its Mission
msg: The final part of Paper 59 deals with the Permian period of biologic tribulation. At that time, as the climate changed abruptly and countless marine creatures perished, the long Paleozoic era came to a close. Today's passage, standing at that very end, looks back on what the sea had done. The vast oceanic nursery of life on Urantia has served its purpose. During the long ages when the land was unsuited to support life, before the atmosphere contained sufficient oxygen to sustain the higher land animals, the sea mothered and nurtured the early life of the realm.

There is warm gratitude in these words. The Life Carrier describes the sea not as a mere physical environment but as a mother who bore and raised life. For hundreds of millions of years the sea sheltered and fed fragile living things and helped them grow into more complex forms. The fact that our blood carries a salinity much like that of sea water bears witness to this ancient bond (see 58:1.4). We are all descendants of the life that grew up in that cradle.

But now, the passage says, the biologic importance of the sea progressively diminishes as the second stage of evolution begins to unfold on the land. A cradle has finished its work when the baby grows up. That is not failure but success. Because the sea had fulfilled its mission completely, it could make way for the next stage. Life left the sea, climbed onto the land, and began a new adventure there. The completion of one stage becoming the beginning of the next: this is the beautiful rhythm of evolution. The Life Carriers looked upon this change not with regret but with expectation. For them evolution was not a static completion but an unceasing process of advance, and the end of each stage was always a door to new possibilities.

This story brings to mind many scenes of our own lives. Parents hold and raise their children, but when the children grow up, they must let them go. Teachers teach their students, but when the students can stand on their own, the teachers must step back. For any community or work, a time comes when, having fulfilled the mission of one season, it must open the way to a new form. Rather than feeling hurt that one's role is shrinking, the mature attitude is to rejoice that the mission has been fulfilled. This was the very spirit of John the Baptist when he confessed, he must increase, but I must decrease.

The same principle applies to the spiritual life. The forms of faith we had as children, habits and understandings that were once a great strength, served as cradles that cared for us. But as the soul grows, a time comes to go out into a wider world. The Urantia Book teaches that the whole ascension journey is an unbroken succession of growth and graduation. Earthly life is the cradle of the morontia life, and the morontia life is the cradle of the spirit life. Each stage nurtures us for the next, and we go on to what follows with gratitude.

Today, call to mind the cradles that raised you. There will be parents, a hometown, a first community of faith, the teachers who taught you. Give thanks for them, and consider whether you can now become such a cradle for someone else. And ask for a generous heart that can gladly let go when the time comes. Gratitude and letting go walk together.
d119.pr: Give thanks for one person or community that nurtured you, and consider how you might become a cradle for someone else.

msg: Paper 60 deals with the early land-life era, the age when reptiles and dinosaurs ruled the earth. But this paper does not plunge straight into the dramatic story of the dinosaurs; it first looks back on the end of the preceding era. Today's passage describes that turning point. The closing epochs of the preceding era were indeed the age of frogs, but these ancestors of the land vertebrates were no longer dominant, having survived in greatly reduced numbers. Very few types outlived the rigorous trials of the preceding period of biologic tribulation. Even the spore-bearing plants were nearly extinct.

This brief record holds the fact that the history of life was never smooth. As we saw in the previous paper, the climatic changes of the Permian swept away vast numbers of living things (see 59:6.2). Flourishing species vanished, and only a very few survived. Evolution looks like an unbroken upward march, but in reality it was a repeated cycle of trial, extinction, and recovery. Life advanced by falling and rising again, over and over. And from the few lives that endured those trials blossomed the abundant life of the next age.

This fact changes the way we view the trials of our own lives. We too pass through times when everything seems to collapse. We lose our health, say goodbye to someone we love, or see in a moment the loss of what we had built up over many years. At such times we become like those frogs, greatly reduced in number and barely surviving. But the history of life shows that it is precisely from such places of bare survival that a new age begins. Trial need not be the end; it can become purification and preparation for the next stage. In the midst of trial it feels like the end, but looking back after time has passed, we often find that it was the threshold of a new beginning.

The Urantia Book does not say that suffering is good in itself. But it teaches that character is tempered through hardship and that true values are revealed in adversity. It explains that uncertainty and difficulty provide a needed stimulus to evolving mortals (see Paper 3). Where there is only comfort, courage, patience, and faith find it hard to grow. Just as life moved on into stronger forms through trial, our souls too grow deeper as we pass through difficulty. To endure trial is not simply to hold on, but to gain new strength within it.

This passage also makes us consider the preciousness of the surviving few. Because a few types survived when most had perished, the stream of life was not broken. In our lives too, when it seems we have lost everything, small things remain: a single friend, a ray of hope, a small faith that has not gone out. When we hold those small things dear, they become the seeds that raise up our whole life again. God is the one who brings forth new shoots even from a remaining stump.

If you are passing through a time of trial today, recall the long history of life. Countless lives fell, yet life itself never stopped. Count with gratitude the small things that remain to you now, and holding on to them, take one more step forward. The Universal Father is already preparing a new age beyond the trial.
d120.pr: Write down three precious things that remain to you even in hard times, and give thanks for them.

msg: The second section of Paper 60 deals with the later reptilian age. Dinosaurs spread out over land, sea, and sky and evolved into many forms. Today's passage tells the story of the reptiles that took to the air, the pterosaurs. Soon after two species of dinosaurs migrated to the water in a futile attempt at self-preservation, two other types were driven to the air by the bitter competition of life on land. These flying pterosaurs had great batlike wings, and for a time they appeared to be a success.

But the passage states plainly that they were not the ancestors of the true birds of subsequent ages. They evolved from the hollow-boned leaping dinosaurs; their wings spread twenty feet and more, and they had jaws much like those of snakes. For a while they seemed to rule the skies, but they failed to evolve along lines which would enable them to survive as air navigators. They represent the nonsurviving strains of bird ancestry. The true birds arose later by an entirely different path, springing directly from a reptilian group (see 60:3.22).

This story makes us think about the difference between outward success and true survival. The pterosaurs once looked like masters of the sky. But their success was not built on a foundation that could last. The path hastily taken under the pressure of competition gave them survival for the moment, but it was not a path leading into the distant future. The first bird, on the other hand, small and pigeonlike, began inconspicuously, yet became the ancestor of all the birds that fill the skies today. Nature shows us in this way that right direction matters more than splendor. Nature sifts life not by haste but by fitness. What endures is not what succeeded fastest but what adapted most rightly. This principle holds true in the spiritual life as well.

Something similar happens in our lives. A path chosen in haste under the push of competition and pressure can look like success for a while. When we hurry to get ahead of others or to avoid falling behind, we may gain immediate results, yet easily miss laying a foundation that will last. The Urantia Book teaches that spiritual growth must be built on true values and right motives. Success founded on selfishness or fear will collapse one day, but growth founded on truth and love leads on into eternity. What survives is what has spiritual value.

This passage also leads us to see that even the lines that failed were not in vain. The pterosaurs disappeared, but their attempt showed that life could reach toward the sky. In the long experiment of the universe, even dead ends are part of the learning. So it is with our own failed attempts. The experience of having taken a wrong road becomes a precious lesson in what road can endure. What matters is to learn from failure and correct our course. God opens new ways even from our dead ends.

Today, reflect on whether the success you are hurrying after rests on a foundation that will last. Examine whether it is a path you chose because you were pushed by others, or out of fear. And make a choice to take one step in the right direction of truth and love, even if no one notices. That small beginning will one day become fruit that fills the sky.
d121.pr: Choose one goal you have been rushing after lately, and quietly examine whether it stands on true values.

msg: Paper 61 deals with the mammalian era on Urantia, the Cenozoic. This period, when the age of dinosaurs ended and mammals began to fill the earth, lasted some fifty million years. Today's passage paints the landscape of that age like a picture. During this Cenozoic age the world's landscape presented an attractive appearance: rolling hills, broad valleys, wide rivers, and great forests. Twice the Panama Isthmus went up and down; three times the Bering Strait land bridge did the same. The trees swarmed with birds, and the animal types were both many and varied.

The last sentence of the passage is especially striking: the whole world was an animal paradise, notwithstanding the incessant struggle of the evolving animal species for supremacy. In these words is the warm gaze of the Life Carrier. Nature was an arena of the struggle for survival, but at the same time it was a garden of rich and beautiful life. A place where competition and beauty, struggle and abundance, mingled together: such was the world just before man appeared. This paradise was also a stage prepared to welcome humankind. We often portray nature solely as a ruthless world where the strong devour the weak, but the heavenly observer saw a paradise within it. The same landscape looks entirely different depending on the eyes that look upon it. Those who look with eyes of love find a festival of life even in the midst of struggle.

This description leads us to reflect on our attitude toward nature. We often see nature as a resource to be used or an obstacle to be overcome. But The Urantia Book shows that the nature of this earth is a work the Life Carriers tended with care for long ages, possessing beauty and value in itself. Paper 56 says that beauty comes from the unification of contrasts (see 56:10.3). A landscape where varied animals and plants, hills, valleys, and rivers blend together is just such an expression of cosmic beauty. In nature we meet the artistry of the Creator.

This passage also reminds us that a world full of competition and conflict can still be beautiful. In the world we live in, quarrels and rivalry never cease. So at times the world seems wholly dark and harsh. But the passage says that despite incessant struggle, the world was a paradise. Conflict does not make beauty disappear. If we lift our eyes, flowers are still blooming, birds are still singing, and good things are still happening among people. We need eyes that see the light within the darkness, rather than letting the darkness capture all our attention.

Recalling the landscape of that age, we feel anew the responsibility human beings bear toward this earth. Before man appeared, this earth was a garden in which countless lives lived together. We are the heirs and stewards who have inherited that garden. On the worlds of light and life that The Urantia Book portrays, human beings live in harmony with nature. To move toward that future, we must cultivate from now on an attitude of respecting and cherishing nature. We must remember that even the smallest life belongs to God's garden.

Today, spend a little time in nature. A park, a forest path, or even a single potted plant by the window will do. Savor slowly the variety and beauty of life there, and give thanks to the Creator who prepared this garden. Then find one way you can become a good steward of this garden.
d122.pr: Spend ten minutes in nature savoring the beauty of life, and decide on one practice of caring for the natural world.
